claims: El Niño and La Niña are opposite phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle in the tropical Pacific.
El Niño is the warm phase.
La Niña is the cool phase.
El Niño brings warmer Pacific waters.
La Niña causes cooler Pacific waters.
El Niño and La Niña typically last 9–12 months.
Recent trends show a shift towards potential El Niño conditions in 2026.
El Niño is called Little Boy.
During El Niño, trade winds weaken.
During El Niño, warm water moves east towards the Americas.
El Niño leads to wetter conditions in the U.S. Gulf Coast.
El Niño leads to warmer/drier conditions in the northern U.S. and Canada.
La Niña is called Little Girl.
During La Niña, trade winds strengthen.
During La Niña, more warm water is pushed west towards Asia.
During La Niña, cooler water is brought to the surface in the east.
La Niña causes drier conditions in the southern U.S.
La Niña causes cooler, wetter weather in the Pacific Northwest.
The current outlook is as of March 2026.
As of March 2026, there was a recent La Niña phase.
As of March 2026, models indicate a likely transition to a neutral state.
As of March 2026, there is a growing probability of El Niño developing.
ENSO events occur every two to seven years.
ENSO events typically last nine to 12 months.
Some ENSO events can persist for multiple years.
During El Niño, there is warmer ocean in the East.
During El Niño, there are warmer/drier conditions in the North USA and wetter conditions in the South USA.
During La Niña, there is cooler ocean in the East.
During La Niña, there are cooler/wetter conditions in the North USA and drier conditions in the South USA.
El Niño and La Niña events are driven by ocean-atmosphere coupling.
Changes in sea surface temperatures (SSTs) alter atmospheric pressure, specifically the Southern Oscillation.
The Southern Oscillation alters the winds that affect ocean temperature, creating a cycle.
